scenes.visual: Title card 'What Keeps Chthamalus High?' over a side-on cartoon of a grey rocky shore with the sea at the bottom. COLOUR MAP, carried over from the first film: TEAL (#0e7c86) = Chthamalus, the species held out (it was species 1's colour); ORANGE (#e57200) = Balanus, the species doing the holding (species 2's colour). Cream background, 16:9. Every number and name appears as on-screen text. All shore, barnacle and whelk drawings are cartoons labelled 'schematic'; barnacles are drawn as simple cones, not anatomy.

scenes.tts: The first film built a test on paper: can a species grow beside its competitor? On a rocky Scottish shore, what keeps one barnacle out of the band just below it?
scenes.visual: A small inset of the first film's phase plane with the white ring shrinks away to the corner. The shore cross-section fills the screen. Label 'Millport, Isle of Cumbrae, Scotland'. A '?' hovers over the boundary between two bands on the rock.
scenes.narration: The first film built a test on paper: can a species grow beside its competitor? On a rocky Scottish shore, what keeps one barnacle out of the band just below it?

scenes.tts: At Millport, adults of the barnacle Chthamalus, in teal, live high on the rock. Another barnacle, Balanus, in orange, covers the rock below. A pattern like that has rival explanations.
scenes.visual: Tide lines are drawn on the rock: 'high tide', 'mid-tide', 'low tide'. A band of small TEAL cones fills in high on the rock, labelled 'Chthamalus'; a dense band of larger ORANGE cones fills in below it, labelled 'Balanus'. The boundary between them is highlighted.
scenes.narration: At Millport, adults of the barnacle Chthamalus, in teal, live high on the rock. Another barnacle, Balanus, in orange, covers the rock below. A pattern like that has rival explanations.

scenes.tts: Lower down, Chthamalus might not tolerate the longer time underwater. Its predators might be worse there, such as the whelk Thais. Or Balanus might be crowding it out.
scenes.visual: Three icons pop up one at a time beside the lower band as each is named: a water drop with a clock 'longer immersion'; a cartoon whelk 'predator: Thais'; ORANGE cones pressing on a TEAL cone 'crowding by Balanus'. Each gets a small '?' tag.
scenes.narration: Lower down, Chthamalus might not tolerate the longer time underwater. Its predators might be worse there, such as the whelk Thais. Or Balanus might be crowding it out.

scenes.tts: Joseph Connell tested the crowding explanation by changing it. He mapped patches of Chthamalus and split each map in two. A coin toss chose one half for removal.
scenes.visual: Zoom into one rock patch seen from above, with marked TEAL cones each with a tiny number and ORANGE cones around them. A dashed line splits the map into two halves. A coin flips; it lands and one half lights up, labelled 'remove Balanus'; the other is labelled 'untouched'. Small corner text: 'Study published 1961'.
scenes.narration: Joseph Connell tested the crowding explanation by changing it. He mapped patches of Chthamalus and split each map in two. A coin toss chose one half for removal.

scenes.tts: On that half, he removed every Balanus touching or surrounding a Chthamalus. The other half stayed untouched, with its Balanus in place, at the same height and in the same weather.
scenes.visual: On the lit half, ORANGE cones touching or surrounding each TEAL cone are lifted away one by one, leaving bare rock around the TEAL cones. The other half keeps its ORANGE cones. A bracket spans both halves: 'same height, same tide, same weather'.
scenes.narration: On that half, he removed every Balanus touching or surrounding a Chthamalus. The other half stayed untouched, with its Balanus in place, at the same height and in the same weather.

scenes.tts: Then he came back at intervals and recounted the marked barnacles on both halves. The difference he intended between the halves was whether Balanus was there.
scenes.visual: A calendar flips several pages. On each visit, the numbered TEAL cones are ticked off on a clipboard tally for each half. Label under the bracket: 'intended difference: Balanus present or removed'.
scenes.narration: Then he came back at intervals and recounted the marked barnacles on both halves. The difference he intended between the halves was whether Balanus was there.

scenes.tts: Suppose longer time underwater was what killed Chthamalus low on the shore, and Balanus did nothing. What would the cleared half show, compared with the untouched half?
scenes.visual: The water-drop-and-clock icon enlarges over both halves equally. Two empty survival bars appear below, labelled 'cleared half' and 'untouched half', with a '?' over each.
scenes.narration: Suppose longer time underwater was what killed Chthamalus low on the shore, and Balanus did nothing. What would the cleared half show, compared with the untouched half?

scenes.visual: Frozen frame. On-screen: 'Better, worse, or the same?' with a 5-second countdown ring.

scenes.tts: If immersion were the cause, both halves would do the same, since both spend the same time underwater. That is not what Connell found. Chthamalus kept free of Balanus survived well, at the shore levels he studied.
scenes.visual: First a ghost pair of equal bars is drawn, labelled 'if immersion were the cause' (schematic). Then they are replaced by the real direction: the 'cleared half' TEAL bar stands tall, the 'untouched half' TEAL bar is short (schematic heights, no values). Label 'removing Balanus helped Chthamalus'. The immersion icon gets a small cross.
scenes.narration: If immersion were the cause, both halves would do the same, since both spend the same time underwater. That is not what Connell found. Chthamalus kept free of Balanus survived well, at the shore levels he studied.

scenes.tts: He also watched how Chthamalus died. Growing Balanus smothered it, undercut it and crushed it. That is interference competition, one barnacle acting directly on another, much of it for space on the rock.
scenes.visual: Close-up on the untouched half in three quick cartoon panels: an ORANGE cone growing over a TEAL one ('smother'), an ORANGE cone growing underneath and lifting a TEAL one off the rock ('undercut'), and two ORANGE cones squeezing a TEAL one ('crush'). Tag: 'direct competition for space'.
scenes.narration: He also watched how Chthamalus died. Growing Balanus smothered it, undercut it and crushed it. That is interference competition, one barnacle acting directly on another, much of it for space on the rock.

scenes.tts: So at Millport, Balanus set the lower limit of Chthamalus. The band where Chthamalus could live reaches lower than the band where it does live. Those are its fundamental and realized niches.
scenes.visual: Back to the shore cross-section. A pale TEAL dashed outline extends the Chthamalus band down into the Balanus zone, labelled 'fundamental niche: where it could live, with no competitors or enemies'. The solid TEAL band is labelled 'realized niche: where it does live, beside Balanus'. An ORANGE bracket marks the gap: 'held out by Balanus'.
scenes.narration: So at Millport, Balanus set the lower limit of Chthamalus. The band where Chthamalus could live reaches lower than the band where it does live. Those are its fundamental and realized niches.

scenes.tts: Keep the scope. This is one shore, one pair of species and one set of years. It does not say what sets barnacle limits on every coast. Its strength is the design, not the generality.
scenes.visual: The shore shrinks to a single pin on an outline map of Scotland's west coast, labelled 'one shore'. Small grey question marks appear at other coast pins: 'other shores: not tested here'.
scenes.narration: Keep the scope. This is one shore, one pair of species and one set of years. It does not say what sets barnacle limits on every coast. Its strength is the design, not the generality.

scenes.tts: For a neighbour that stays put, like a barnacle, the design gives a field test. Remove it from a random half, and leave a matched half alone. If survival improves, and proper controls rule out other differences, the neighbour was limiting.
scenes.visual: A generic split-patch icon: one half with a neighbour removed, one untouched, a coin above. TEAL survival tally bars: taller on the removal side. Text: 'randomized removal + untouched comparison + controls'.
scenes.narration: For a neighbour that stays put, like a barnacle, the design gives a field test. Remove it from a random half, and leave a matched half alone. If survival improves, and proper controls rule out other differences, the neighbour was limiting.

scenes.visual: End card with the Hex mascot beside a TEAL barnacle cone on bare rock. Take-home line: 'Randomized, controlled removal: better survival is evidence the neighbour was limiting.'
